about.intro: I grew up in Larchmont Falls and studied commerce at Ashgrove College, where I ran the posters for every society and got the print shop to give me a student rate. I joined Pinewick Paper & Print in 2019 as a marketing coordinator and stayed six years: first catalogues and price sheets, then campaigns, then the brand and growth team. Our regional manager, Gordie Pruitt, believed any problem could be solved with a four-letter acronym on a whiteboard, so I learned to bring a number as well as a slogan. In 2022 I started Shopfront Sundays, a reel series on the valley's last independent stationery counters. I joined Millbrook School of Management in 2025 to move to a brand where I own the budget as well as the content.
about.now: Filming a Stonebridge edition of Shopfront Sundays each weekend, five-a-side football on Tuesday evenings, and a weekly newsletter called Copy That that takes apart one small-brand ad.

glow-creators.context: Longline is a refillable gel pen that Pinewick launched in March 2024. Pen ads here usually show a swirl on a notebook page, and the company's last launch reels managed 0.8% engagement. Regional manager Gordie Pruitt's brief was one line on a whiteboard: 'LAUNCH = L.O.U.D.'. We wanted something that survived without an acronym.
glow-creators.problem: Buyers assume a refillable pen dies mid-exam and do not trust ink claims. We were after a format that proved the pen lasted, that creators could film at home, and that looked nothing like other pen ads.
glow-creators.my_role: Brand & Growth Lead: idea, creator brief and launch plan were mine
what_i_did: Trialled the format on two creators and on myself: draw an unbroken line along a roll of till paper until the pen gives up, then measure it.
Chose 48 micro-creators with 10k to 80k followers across Larchmont Falls, Stonebridge, Harrowgate, Ashgrove and Millbrook, ranked by the save rate of their last 20 posts rather than follower count.
Wrote a single-page brief: three mandatory shots, no script, and a banned-word list that included 'smooth' and 'buttery'.
Waited 72 hours, then boosted only the six strongest reels using the 40% of paid budget I had kept back.
Kept a weekly tracker of views, saves and code-linked orders for Pinewick and the agency to go through each Monday, with Wendell checking the line lengths.

decisions.choice: Forty-eight small voices, not two famous ones
decisions.why: The same money bought 48 hands and 48 handwriting styles, and stationery micro-creators saved posts about three times as often.

decisions.choice: Keep the moment the ink fades
decisions.why: Reels in which the creator watched the line thin out near the end were saved more than tidy ones, so every creator was asked to leave that bit in.

decisions.choice: Park 40% of paid spend for three days
decisions.why: Nobody could predict which creators would land. A three-day wait let the money follow reels people were already saving.

results.note: organic and boosted, first four weeks
in the first 21 days, Pinewick webshop

glow-creators.learned: Rough till-paper reels shot at kitchen tables reached a 3.9% save rate. Pinewick's polished studio films reached 1.2%.
glow-creators.next: Apply the idea to refills: a mid-term 'is it still going?' check at colleges and offices, where pen loyalty is actually decided.

pav-patrol.context: Shopfront Sundays began in 2022 as a way to practise shooting and editing in my own time. Each week it features one stationery counter in the Larch Valley, and since 2025 a Stonebridge one as well.
pav-patrol.problem: Local shop pages mostly post prices and offers. Owners said they felt reduced to a stock list, and the reels blurred together, so I looked for a format that people would pass on for the owner's sake as much as the shelves.
what_i_did: Fixed the format: under 40 seconds, owner's name and opening year in the first frame, plus a line the owner said, quoted as spoken.
Filmed each reel in under an hour with a phone and small gimbal, and cut it in DaVinci Resolve on Sunday mornings.
Recorded every reel in a spreadsheet: hook, length, shop type, and views, saves and shares for the next seven days.
From 2023 accepted paid collaborations under one rule: a brand reel after every four counter reels, and brands never appear inside a counter reel.

decisions.why: Once I stopped filming the stock list, owners relaxed and posted the reels on their own pages.

decisions.choice: Open on the person, not the shelf
decisions.why: My logs show owner-first reels earned 2.4 times the shares of shelf-first ones.

pav-patrol.learned: For a small page, shares beat views. Shares bring back followers who stay, whereas explore-page views mostly vanish.
pav-patrol.next: Publish the shared map of counters that followers keep requesting, and build a Stonebridge series the same way.

twt-creator-test.context: Kettleby Pantry brought out a new oat bar flavour in early 2026. The brand's own site sold it well, yet on quick-commerce apps, where new shoppers first meet the brand, it crawled.
twt-creator-test.problem: Brand-made ads for the bar earned a 1.7% click-through on Instagram, while the cost of each quick-commerce order in Harrowgate and Stonebridge sat well above target.
twt-creator-test.my_role: Brand Marketing Intern: designed the test and wrote the creator brief
what_i_did: Read 300 reviews and comments about the bar to learn how buyers describe it; 'tastes like a biscuit' and 'keeps me going till lunch' appeared most.
Gave 18 fitness and food creators in Harrowgate and Stonebridge using a two-line hook lifted from those comments, with no script.
Agreed with the performance team to run creator reels and brand ads side by side for three weeks, sharing budget, audience and landing page.
Followed the funnel from views through to orders in a single spreadsheet, and filmed two creator sessions personally.
Gave the marketing head a readout proposing to shift 30% of the quick-commerce budget into creator reels.

decisions.why: The brand wrote about ingredients; buyers wrote about taste first. Taste-led hooks won within a week.

decisions.choice: Identical budget and audience in each arm
decisions.why: Otherwise targeting, not creative, could explain any difference.

results.note: creator reels against brand ads, 3 weeks

twt-creator-test.learned: Reels with the least polish performed best. Creators who ate the bar on their walk to work outdid those who staged a flat lay.
twt-creator-test.next: Try the winning hooks as quick-commerce banner ads, where creator faces have not appeared yet.

brief_me.title: Brief me
brief_me.intro: Choose a goal, a budget and your channels. The sketch that prints is assembled from my earlier work: the nearest case, the format I would open with and the figure I would track.

goals.label: Awareness
goals.metric: Saves plus shares for every 1,000 views
goals.metric_why: Reach is cheap on Reels. Saves and shares show people want to return to the post.

goals.label: Launch
goals.metric: Creator-code orders during the first 30 days
goals.metric_why: Each creator gets tied to sales, so extra spend backs the ones that actually sell.

goals.label: Sales
goals.metric: Cost per order compared with your own ads
goals.metric_why: Give both the same budget and audience, and any difference is down to the creative alone.

budget.label: Budget for the first eight weeks

holdback.text: kept in reserve for 72 hours, then pushed behind whatever is already working

bands.plan: Small budget: start with 10 to 15 micro-creators chosen by save rate, and skip the production shoot.
Medium budget: roughly 25 to 50 micro-creators spread over four or five towns, plus a head-to-head against your own ads.
Large budget: a full creator programme and one hero film, which is then chopped into the ads that earn their keep.
